patient.name: Errol Campbell
patient.setting: GP surgery, then the urology clinic and oncology ward
patient.complaint: Three months of low back pain and losing weight without trying
background: Jamaican heritage; retired electrician in Brixton
Brother treated for prostate cancer at 62

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an older man, a hard irregular prostate and a high PSA, or a man with known prostate cancer and back pain or leg weakness (bone metastases, cord compression).

points: Errol, 67: dull **low back pain** for 3 months, worse at night.
Mild nocturia, but no real change in his stream.

steps.lead: Errol has two risk factors already: **Afro-Caribbean** heritage and a strong family history.

points: Tender over L3 on spinal percussion.

steps.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: A **hard, irregular, asymmetric** prostate with loss of the sulcus, weight loss and bone pain is prostate cancer until proven otherwise.

steps.lead: Errol's tumour sits in the **peripheral zone**, which is the part a finger on DRE can feel.
His PSA comes back **markedly** raised. Note his stream is fine: cancer does not usually cause early obstruction.

visual.title: Errol's PSA
visual.label: Errol 48
visual.caption: BPH gives a normal or mildly raised PSA. A PSA of 48 with a hard gland points to cancer.

steps.title: BPH or prostate cancer?
head: Feature
BPH
Prostate cancer
rows: Weight loss, bone pain, clot retention

steps.lead: Errol's night-time back pain is a warning of **osteoblastic spinal metastases**, the route to cord compression.

steps.text: Back pain plus new **leg weakness, sensory loss or bladder or bowel change** in prostate cancer is **metastatic spinal cord compression** until proven otherwise.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate next investigation?' (2WW referral with multiparametric MRI), 'Which confirms the diagnosis?' (biopsy with Gleason grading) and 'Which investigation for suspected cord compression?' (urgent MRI spine).

steps.lead: Errol's hard prostate meets NICE criteria for an urgent **2-week-wait** referral, with a PSA sent alongside.

steps.q: What is the first imaging test after referral?
steps.r: **Multiparametric MRI** comes first; the PI-RADS score decides whether a biopsy is needed.

steps.lead: Errol's PI-RADS 5 lesion is biopsied: **Gleason 4 + 4 = 8**, which is high grade.

visual.title: Gleason score
visual.label: Errol 4+4=8
visual.caption: The first number is the most common pattern. Higher scores mean worse prognosis.

steps.lead: Three tools run Errol's work-up: **NICE referral** criteria, **PI-RADS** on MRI and **Gleason** grading on biopsy.
Bone is the commonest site of spread, so Errol is staged with **CT and a bone scan**.

steps.title: Errol's staging bloods and scans
rows: Hot spots L3, L4 and pelvis
steps.text: A high ALP with normal calcium fits **osteoblastic** metastases.

steps.lead: If Errol ever goes into retention, check **creatinine**; after treatment his PSA tracks response; and new leg signs mean **urgent MRI spine**.

steps.text: Do not measure PSA within **48 hours** of ejaculation or vigorous exercise, or during a UTI or prostatitis.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' across the spectrum: active surveillance for low risk, radical prostatectomy for fit high-risk localised disease, ADT with anti-androgen cover for metastatic disease, and urgent MRI with decompression for cord compression.

steps.q: Errol has Gleason 8 with bone metastases. What is the main treatment?
steps.r: Metastatic (advanced) disease is treated with **androgen deprivation therapy**; surgery and brachytherapy are for localised disease.

steps.title: Choosing treatment
nodes: Low grade, low PSA, localised: active surveillance
Low risk but life expectancy <10 years: watchful waiting
Fit, high-risk localised (Gleason ≥8, PSA >20, >T2c): radical prostatectomy (RALP)

steps.lead: If Errol's cancer had been small and low grade, he would have been offered **active surveillance** instead.
Had Errol's high-grade cancer been confined to the prostate, a fit man like him would be offered **RALP**.
With bone metastases, Errol starts **goserelin**, covered by an anti-androgen first so the flare does not hit his spine.

steps.text: Starting goserelin **without** anti-androgen cover in a man with spinal metastases can cause flare, bone pain and **cord compression**.

visual.title: Errol's PSA on androgen deprivation
visual.caption: PSA is used to monitor response; a later rise suggests progression.

points: Fourteen months later: worse back pain for a week.
Today: legs feel heavy; he stumbles on the stairs.
Numb from the waist down; has not passed urine since morning.

o: Increase his analgesia and review in a week
steps.r: New leg weakness, sensory level and retention in a man with spinal metastases is **MSCC**: urgent MRI spine.

steps.lead: Errol's MRI shows cord compression at T12. He gets dexamethasone and is reviewed for **surgical decompression** or radiotherapy.

science.exam: Science questions ask why prostate metastases are osteoblastic, why PSA is not cancer-specific, why Gleason predicts prognosis and why goserelin causes a tumour flare.

steps.lead: Errol's cancer grew in the **peripheral zone**, which explains the hard nodule on DRE and why his stream stayed normal.
Errol's PSA of 48 reflects glandular disruption by cancer, but PSA also rises with **BPH, prostatitis and instrumentation**.

steps.q: Which of these would also raise PSA in a man without cancer?
steps.r: Instrumentation, biopsy, prostatitis, UTI and ejaculation all raise PSA. Finasteride **lowers** it.

steps.lead: Errol's pattern 4 means fused, poorly formed glands: **less normal architecture, worse prognosis**.
Errol's bone scan lit up because his tumour **stimulates osteoblasts**, giving sclerotic, not lytic, lesions.
Goserelin first **stimulates** then switches off pituitary GnRH receptors, so Errol needed anti-androgen cover.

visual.title: Testosterone after starting goserelin
visual.caption: The early **surge** is the tumour flare; castrate levels follow once receptors downregulate.

mcq.q: In which zone do most prostate adenocarcinomas arise?
mcq.r: Over **75%** arise in the peripheral zone.

mcq.q: Which is a recognised risk factor for prostate cancer?
What type of bone metastases does prostate cancer cause?
What is the upper limit of normal PSA used in the notes?
What is the first-line imaging for suspected prostate cancer?
At what PI-RADS score is biopsy indicated?
What is the gold-standard investigation for suspected spinal cord compression?
What is first-line treatment for fit men with high-risk localised disease?
Which drug is given before goserelin to prevent tumour flare?
Why does goserelin cause a tumour flare?

technique.stem: A 69 year old Afro-Caribbean man has a 2 month history of low back pain that wakes him at night and 5 kg weight loss. His urinary stream is normal. Digital rectal examination shows a hard, irregular, asymmetric prostate with loss of the median sulcus. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: the DRE description and PSA usually decide it.
Risk group, red flags (night pain, weight loss), and a malignant-feeling gland with markedly raised PSA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Prostate cancer** with probable bone metastases.

elim: BPH gives a smooth, firm gland and obstructive LUTS.
Bladder cancer presents with painless haematuria; the prostate is normal.
Prostatitis gives pelvic pain and a tender, boggy gland.
Myeloma causes bone pain but not an abnormal prostate, and PSA would be normal.

steps.x: **E. Prostate cancer.** Rule: hard and irregular with a lost sulcus = cancer; smooth = BPH.

technique.stem: A 74 year old man with prostate cancer and known spinal metastases has had worsening thoracic back pain for a week. Today he has bilateral leg weakness and numbness below the umbilicus. He has not passed urine for 8 hours. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 148/88 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Plain X-ray of the thoracic spine

steps.x: An investigation question in an emergency: which test shows the cord?
Spinal metastases plus weakness, a sensory level and retention: metastatic spinal cord compression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent MRI whole spine.**

elim: A bone scan shows metastases but not cord compression.
The signs are spinal (sensory level), not cerebral.
These assess peripheral nerves, not the cord.
X-ray can miss compression and cannot show the cord.

steps.x: **E. Urgent MRI whole spine.** Rule: suspected MSCC = MRI within hours.

technique.stem: A 61 year old man has a PSA of 5.2 µg/L. MRI shows a PI-RADS 3 lesion confined to the prostate. Biopsy shows Gleason 3 + 3 = 6 adenocarcinoma in one core. Staging shows no spread. He is fit and works full time. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management: grade and stage decide it.
Low grade, low PSA, localised.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Active surveillance**: regular PSA, MRI and repeat biopsy.

elim: ADT is for advanced or metastatic disease.
Chemotherapy is for metastatic disease.
Radical surgery is for high-risk localised disease (Gleason ≥8, PSA >20).
TURP treats BPH obstruction, not cancer.

steps.x: **A. Active surveillance.** Rule: low risk = surveillance; high-risk localised = RALP; metastatic = ADT.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man with prostate cancer has pain in his lower back. X-ray of the lumbar spine shows dense white areas in L2 and L4. His ALP is 340 U/L (30–130) and adjusted calcium 2.41 mmol/L (2.20–2.60).
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the bone lesions?
o: Decreased bone mineralisation from vitamin D deficiency
Increased osteoclast activity from PTH-related peptide

steps.x: A mechanism question explaining a finding: dense, white (sclerotic) lesions.
Sclerotic lesions, high ALP, normal calcium: osteoblastic metastases.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Tumour cells **stimulate osteoblasts**, laying down new abnormal bone.

elim: That is osteomalacia, with low calcium and Looser zones.
That causes lytic lesions and hypercalcaemia.
That is myeloma, which gives lytic lesions.
That causes osteoporosis, not dense patches.

steps.x: **E. Tumour-driven stimulation of osteoblast activity.** Prostate = blastic; breast and myeloma = lytic.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has a 3 month history of tiredness and 4 kg weight loss. Digital rectal examination shows a hard, nodular, irregular prostate. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A hard, irregular prostate with weight loss and a PSA of 34 is prostate cancer. BPH gives a smooth gland and a normal or mildly raised PSA.

steps.x: Diagnosis from the DRE and the PSA.
Weight loss, malignant-feeling prostate, PSA markedly raised.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Prostate cancer.**

elim: BPH is smooth, with normal or mildly raised PSA.
Bladder cancer gives haematuria and a normal prostate.
Prostatitis is painful, with a tender gland.
A rectal tumour is felt in the rectal wall, not as a hard prostate, and PSA would be normal.

steps.x: **D. Prostate cancer.**

practice.stem: A 64 year old Black British man has a PSA of 16 µg/L (<4) on a routine check. He has no urinary symptoms. His brother had prostate cancer at 58. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on digital rectal examination?
o: Hard, irregular, asymmetric prostate with loss of the central sulcus
Normal rectal examination with an empty rectum
Soft rectal mass separate from the prostate
practice.e: Peripheral zone cancer is felt on DRE as a hard, irregular, asymmetric gland with loss of the sulcus. Smooth enlargement is BPH.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question: predict the DRE from the risk and PSA.
High-risk ethnicity and family history, markedly raised PSA, no obstruction: peripheral zone cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hard, irregular, asymmetric prostate**, central sulcus lost.

elim: That is acute prostatitis.
A PSA of 16 with this risk profile makes an abnormal gland likely.
That is BPH, which would give LUTS and a normal or mildly raised PSA.
That suggests a rectal lesion.

steps.x: **B. Hard, irregular, asymmetric prostate.**

practice.stem: A 75 year old man with prostate cancer has 2 months of lumbar back pain. Neurological examination of the legs is normal. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray of the lumbar spine?
practice.e: Prostate bone metastases are osteoblastic (sclerotic) with a raised ALP. Lytic punched-out lesions suggest myeloma or breast cancer.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question: what do prostate bone metastases look like?
Prostate cancer with back pain, raised ALP, normal calcium.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sclerotic (osteoblastic) metastases.**

elim: Osteopenia is osteoporosis or osteomalacia, not metastases.
Lytic lesions are typical of myeloma and breast metastases.
These are seen in hyperparathyroidism.
These are seen in ankylosing spondylitis.

steps.x: **C. Sclerotic (osteoblastic) lesions.**

practice.stem: A 72 year old man with prostate cancer and bone metastases has had increasing back pain for 2 weeks. For 2 days he has had difficulty walking and reduced sensation in both legs. He has new urinary incontinence. Power is 3/5 in both legs. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 150/90 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Back pain with bilateral leg weakness, sensory loss and incontinence in a man with prostate bone metastases is metastatic spinal cord compression.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a man with known metastases and new neurology.
Bone metastases, back pain, bilateral weakness, sensory loss and bladder dysfunction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Metastatic spinal cord compression.**

elim: GBS is an ascending neuropathy after infection, without back pain or a sensory level.
Hypercalcaemia causes confusion and constipation, not focal leg weakness.
Stroke is sudden and usually one-sided.
Neuropathy is slow, distal and does not cause new incontinence.

steps.x: **D. Metastatic spinal cord compression.** Urgent MRI spine next.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer started goserelin 6 days ago. He was not given any other new drug. He now has worsening bone pain in his spine and pelvis and difficulty passing urine. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 140/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
practice.e: Goserelin without anti-androgen cover causes a transient tumour flare: bone pain, bladder obstruction and risk of cord compression.

steps.x: A cause question: link the timing to the new drug.

clues: not given any other new drug
steps.x: A GnRH agonist started days ago with no anti-androgen cover, then bone pain and obstruction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Tumour flare** from the initial testosterone surge.

elim: Resistance develops over months to years, not 6 days.
His calcium is normal, and prostate metastases are blastic.
He has not started an opioid.
There is no fever, and the dipstick is negative.

steps.x: **D. Tumour flare from goserelin.** Prevent with flutamide or cyproterone acetate first.

practice.stem: A 59 year old White British man asks about his risk of prostate cancer. His sister developed breast cancer at 38 and genetic testing found a pathogenic variant. He has tested positive for the same variant. He does not smoke. His pulse rate is 66 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely factor increasing his risk?
practice.e: BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations increase prostate cancer risk, along with Afro-Caribbean ethnicity. Undescended testis is a testicular cancer risk.

steps.x: A risk-factor question: what does the family history mean?

clues: tested positive for the same variant
steps.x: Early breast cancer in a sister with a shared pathogenic variant: a BRCA mutation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **BRCA2** (BRCA1 also raises risk).

elim: Lynch syndrome is linked mainly to colorectal and endometrial cancer, not early breast cancer.
Vasectomy is not an established risk factor.
He does not smoke, and smoking is not a key risk factor here.
That is a testicular cancer risk factor.

steps.x: **A. BRCA2 mutation.**

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has a hard nodule in the left lobe of his prostate on digital rectal examination. He has no urinary symptoms. He has been referred on the 2-week-wait pathway.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: First-line for suspected prostate cancer is multiparametric MRI scored with PI-RADS; biopsy follows if PI-RADS is 3 or more.

steps.x: Next investigation after a 2WW referral.
Suspected cancer: image first to decide on and target biopsy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Multiparametric MRI prostate**, scored with PI-RADS.

elim: Staging comes after the diagnosis is confirmed.
CT is for staging, not first-line.
A hard nodule and raised PSA need urgent work-up now.
Biopsy follows MRI, guided by PI-RADS.

steps.x: **C. Multiparametric MRI prostate.**

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has a PSA of 11 µg/L (<4) and a firm nodule on digital rectal examination. Multiparametric MRI of the prostate shows a PI-RADS 4 lesion in the right peripheral zone. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
practice.e: PI-RADS 3 or more leads to prostate biopsy, which confirms the diagnosis and gives the Gleason score. Bone scan and CT stage it.

steps.x: Confirming the diagnosis means tissue.
PI-RADS 3 or above means biopsy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Prostate biopsy** (transperineal or TRUS), graded by Gleason.

elim: A bone scan stages spread; it does not confirm cancer.
CT stages; it does not give histology.
PI-RADS 4 needs biopsy now, not repeat imaging.
PSA ratios do not give a tissue diagnosis.

steps.x: **C. Prostate biopsy.**

practice.stem: A 60 year old man has prostate cancer confined to the prostate. Biopsy shows Gleason 4 + 4 = 8. His PSA is 24 µg/L (<4). CT and bone scan show no spread. He is fit and plays tennis weekly. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Fit men with high-risk localised disease (Gleason ≥8 or PSA >20) are offered radical prostatectomy, preferably robot-assisted.

steps.x: Management: grade, PSA, stage and fitness.
High-risk localised disease (Gleason ≥8, PSA >20) in a fit man.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Radical prostatectomy**, favouring RALP.

elim: Surveillance is for low-grade, low-PSA disease.
ADT is for advanced disease.
Chemotherapy is for metastatic disease.
Watchful waiting is for low-risk disease with short life expectancy.

steps.x: **D. Robot-assisted radical prostatectomy.** Warn about incontinence and erectile dysfunction.

practice.stem: A 73 year old man has newly diagnosed prostate cancer with multiple bone metastases on bone scan. The oncology team plans to start goserelin. He has back pain but normal neurology. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to give before starting goserelin?
practice.e: An anti-androgen (cyproterone acetate or flutamide) is started before goserelin to block the effect of the initial testosterone surge.

steps.x: Management detail: what prevents the GnRH agonist flare?
Spinal metastases mean a flare could cause cord compression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: An **anti-androgen** first: cyproterone acetate or flutamide.

elim: Dexamethasone is for established cord compression, not flare prevention.
Finasteride is a BPH drug and does not block androgen receptors.
Tamsulosin treats LUTS, not flare.
A bisphosphonate protects bone but does not stop the testosterone surge.

steps.x: **A. Cyproterone acetate.**

practice.stem: An 84 year old man with severe heart failure and COPD has prostate cancer found after a raised PSA. Biopsy shows Gleason 3 + 3 = 6 and staging shows localised disease. His PSA is 6.1 µg/L (<4). His life expectancy is estimated at under 5 years.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Low-risk prostate cancer with significant comorbidity or life expectancy under 10 years is managed by watchful waiting.

steps.x: Management: weigh the cancer against the man.
Low-risk disease with major comorbidity and short life expectancy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Watchful waiting**: treat symptoms if they appear.

elim: Radiotherapy carries morbidity with little benefit at this risk and life expectancy.
Chemotherapy is for metastatic disease.
ADT is for advanced disease.
He is not fit and has low-risk disease.

steps.x: **E. Watchful waiting.**

practice.stem: A 70 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer starts leuprorelin. Blood tests on day 3 show a testosterone level higher than before treatment. By week 4 his testosterone is at castrate levels.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the early rise in testosterone?
o: Blockade of androgen receptors on tumour cells
Initial stimulation of pituitary GnRH receptors
Loss of negative feedback from oestrogen
practice.e: GnRH agonists first stimulate pituitary receptors (LH and testosterone surge, the flare) and then downregulate them, giving castrate testosterone.

steps.x: A mechanism question explaining a lab pattern.
A GnRH agonist first stimulates then downregulates receptors.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Initial GnRH receptor stimulation** gives an LH and testosterone surge (flare).

elim: That is bicalutamide's action and lowers androgen effect.
That is finasteride; it lowers DHT, not raises testosterone.
Leuprorelin does not act on oestrogen feedback.
Leydig cells do not grow in 3 days.

steps.x: **C. Initial stimulation of pituitary GnRH receptors.**

prompts.q: What is prostate cancer, where does it arise and who gets it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: zone and risk factors are classic recall.

points.p: Usually adenocarcinoma; commonest cancer in UK men
Peripheral zone (>75%)
Afro-Caribbean ethnicity
BRCA1 and BRCA2
points.why: A family history of early breast cancer is the stem clue.

prompts.q: How does prostate cancer present and how is it different from BPH?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the DRE description gives it away.

points.p: Hard, irregular, asymmetric prostate with loss of central sulcus
Markedly raised PSA
points.why: BPH is normal or mildly raised.

points.p: Weight loss, clot retention
Does not typically cause acute urinary retention or early LUTS

prompts.q: What are the features of advanced disease and its complications?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: back pain in a man with prostate cancer = bone metastases.

points.p: Osteoblastic bone metastases, often spine
Metastatic spinal cord compression
Pathological fractures and back pain

prompts.q: What are the signs of metastatic spinal cord compression?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: any new neurology plus back pain in metastatic cancer.

points.p: Limb weakness and difficulty walking
Sensory loss
Bladder or bowel dysfunction

prompts.q: What can raise PSA apart from cancer?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: delay the test if any are present.

points.p: BPH
Prostatitis or UTI
Recent ejaculation or vigorous exercise
Instrumentation, catheter, retention

prompts.q: What is the diagnostic pathway for suspected prostate cancer?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: MRI comes before biopsy.

points.p: 2WW referral with PSA for a hard, irregular prostate
Multiparametric MRI prostate scored with PI-RADS
PI-RADS ≥3: biopsy (transperineal or TRUS)
Gleason grading

prompts.q: How is the Gleason score built and interpreted?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the first number is the most common pattern.

points.p: Two areas each scored out of 5 and added
≤6 low, 7 intermediate, 8–10 high

prompts.q: How is prostate cancer staged and monitored, and what is the test for cord compression?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: bone is the commonest spread site.

points.p: CT and bone scan for staging
points.why: Osteoblastic lesions show as hot spots.

points.p: PSA every 6–12 months for 5 years after prostatectomy
Urgent MRI spine for suspected MSCC

prompts.q: How is localised prostate cancer managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: low risk = watch; high risk and fit = cut.

points.p: Low grade, low PSA: active surveillance
Low risk, life expectancy <10 years: watchful waiting
Fit, high-risk localised (Gleason ≥8, PSA >20, >T2c): radical prostatectomy, RALP
Radiotherapy or brachytherapy for T2N0M0; risk of proctitis

prompts.q: How is advanced disease managed, and how is cord compression treated?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: never start goserelin without cover.

points.p: Androgen deprivation therapy: GnRH agonist (goserelin, leuprorelin) or anti-androgen (bicalutamide)
Anti-androgen cover first: flutamide or cyproterone acetate
MSCC: urgent MRI spine, surgical decompression
points.why: Plus steroids and radiotherapy in practice.

prompts.q: Why are prostate metastases osteoblastic, and why does goserelin cause a flare?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: blastic = prostate; lytic = breast or myeloma.

points.p: Tumour stimulates osteoblast activity, giving sclerotic lesions
GnRH agonists first stimulate then downregulate pituitary receptors
Gleason reflects loss of glandular architecture

glossary.adenocarcinoma: Cancer arising from glandular epithelium; the usual type of prostate cancer.
glossary.peripheral zone: The outer posterior part of the prostate, felt on DRE, where most cancers arise.
glossary.transition zone: The part of the prostate surrounding the urethra, where BPH arises.
glossary.central sulcus: The groove between the two prostate lobes; lost when cancer spreads across the gland.
glossary.median sulcus: Another name for the central sulcus of the prostate.
glossary.DRE: Digital rectal examination: feeling the prostate through the rectal wall.
glossary.PSA: Prostate specific antigen: a serine protease from prostate cells; normal below 4.
glossary.BRCA2: A tumour suppressor gene; mutations raise the risk of breast, ovarian and prostate cancer.
glossary.BRCA1: A tumour suppressor gene; mutations raise breast, ovarian and prostate cancer risk.
glossary.2WW: Two-week-wait: NICE urgent referral pathway for suspected cancer.
glossary.multiparametric MRI: MRI combining several sequences to find and score suspicious prostate lesions.
glossary.PI-RADS: Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System: scores MRI lesions 1 to 5; 3 or above means biopsy.
glossary.TRUS: Transrectal ultrasound, used to guide prostate biopsy.
glossary.transperineal biopsy: Prostate biopsy through the skin between scrotum and anus, with lower infection risk.
glossary.Gleason score: Sum of the two commonest histological patterns (each 1 to 5); 8 to 10 is high grade.
glossary.bone scan: Isotope scan showing areas of high bone turnover, such as metastases.
glossary.osteoblastic: Bone-forming; prostate metastases lay down dense, sclerotic bone.
glossary.osteolytic: Bone-destroying; lytic lesions look like holes on X-ray.
glossary.ALP: Alkaline phosphatase: an enzyme raised when bone turnover is high.
glossary.MSCC: Metastatic spinal cord compression: an oncological emergency causing back pain and leg weakness.
glossary.spinal cord compression: Pressure on the cord causing weakness, sensory loss and bladder or bowel dysfunction.
glossary.active surveillance: Monitoring low-risk cancer with PSA, MRI and biopsy, treating only if it progresses.
glossary.watchful waiting: Treating symptoms only, for men whose cancer is unlikely to shorten their life.
glossary.radical prostatectomy: Surgical removal of the whole prostate and seminal vesicles.
glossary.brachytherapy: Radiotherapy given by implanting radioactive seeds in the prostate.
glossary.proctitis: Inflammation of the rectum, e.g. after radiotherapy: bloody diarrhoea and tenesmus.
glossary.tenesmus: A constant feeling of needing to open the bowels.
glossary.androgen deprivation therapy: Treatment that removes or blocks testosterone to slow prostate cancer.
glossary.GnRH agonist: Drug that first stimulates, then switches off, the pituitary's GnRH receptors.
glossary.goserelin: A GnRH agonist implant used for advanced prostate cancer.
glossary.leuprorelin: A GnRH agonist used for advanced prostate cancer.
glossary.bicalutamide: An anti-androgen that blocks androgen receptors.
glossary.anti-androgen: Drug that blocks androgen receptors, e.g. bicalutamide, flutamide, cyproterone.
glossary.flutamide: An anti-androgen used to cover the goserelin flare.
glossary.cyproterone acetate: An anti-androgen used to prevent tumour flare when starting a GnRH agonist.
glossary.tumour flare: Temporary worsening of cancer from the testosterone surge when a GnRH agonist starts.
glossary.clot retention: Inability to pass urine because blood clots block the urethra.
glossary.TNM: Tumour, Node, Metastasis staging system, e.g. T2N0M0.
